content.text: A moment is the turning effect of a force. When you push a door, use a spanner, or sit on a seesaw, you're using moments. Understanding moments helps us analyse balanced systems and design structures that don't topple.

A moment is the turning effect of a force about a pivot point. It depends on two things: the size of the force AND the perpendicular distance from the pivot. Moment = Force x perpendicular distance (N m).

content.text: For a system in equilibrium (balanced), the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about that point.

The principle of moments states: for a balanced (equilibrium) system, the sum of clockwise moments = the sum of anticlockwise moments about any point. This is the key equation for solving seesaw and lever problems.

content.text: When calculating moments, always use the PERPENDICULAR distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. If the force is applied at an angle, the effective distance is shorter than the actual distance along the lever.
— Moment depends on force AND distance. A small force far from the pivot can balance a large force near the pivot.
— Distance is measured perpendicular from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
— Clockwise and anticlockwise moments oppose each other. They must be treated as opposite signs.
"Centre of mass is always inside the object"
— For objects with holes (like a ring), centre of mass can be in empty space.
— Stability depends on centre of mass position and base width, not just weight.
